questions.prompt: Which line makes this translation unit ill-formed?
questions.explanation: Floating to integer is a narrowing conversion, and narrowing is banned only in list-initialization. (C) is list-initialization from a `double`, so it is ill-formed. (A) and (B) perform the same conversion with `=` and parentheses, which is allowed and truncates to 3. (D) is also list-initialization, but from the `int` constant 3, which needs no conversion.

Reaching `std::string` needs its converting constructor, a user-defined conversion sequence. A standard conversion sequence always ranks better than a user-defined one, so `f(bool)` wins and there is no ambiguity.

A promotion ranks better than a conversion, so `f(double)` is chosen. questions.prompt: Which of these declarations are well-formed?
questions.explanation: `n1` is copy-initialization from `const char[4]`, which needs a single implicit conversion all the way to `Name`: `const char*` to `std::string` and then `std::string` to `Name`, two user-defined conversions, so it is ill-formed. `n2` and `n3` select `Name`'s constructor by overload resolution, so the only implicit conversion left is the argument to `std::string`, which needs just one. Copy-list-initialization is the tempting exception people forget: it calls the constructor directly too.

questions.prompt: With `CHAR_BIT == 8`, which of these braced initializations are well-formed?
options: All three: each value fits or is converted modulo 2^8
questions.explanation: `int` to `char` is narrowing unless the source is a constant expression whose value fits. `i` is not a constant expression, so `c1` is ill-formed even though 10 would fit at run time; GCC only warns about it by default, while Clang rejects it. `k` is a constant 10, so `c2` is fine. `big` is a constant, but 300 does not fit in an 8-bit `signed char`, so `c3` is ill-formed.

questions.prompt: In C++20 or later, which of these initializations are ill-formed?
questions.explanation: P1957, adopted for C++20 as a defect report, made pointer and pointer-to-member to `bool` a narrowing conversion, so it is banned in the braces of `b2`. It is still an ordinary implicit boolean conversion, so `b1` is fine. `b3` contextually converts `p` for `!` and then initializes from a `bool`, which needs no conversion at all. GCC diagnoses `b2` only with a warning by default; Clang rejects it.

questions.prompt: In C++23, which declaration is ill-formed?
questions.explanation: The operand of a `noexcept` specifier is a contextually converted constant expression of type `bool`, and converted constant expressions forbid narrowing; `int` 2 to `bool` is narrowing because `bool` cannot represent 2. C++23 (P1401) relaxed exactly two such contexts, `static_assert` and `if constexpr`, to plain contextual conversion, so the first and third options are valid. `bool b = 2;` is ordinary copy-initialization, where narrowing is allowed.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what does the standard say about this code?
questions.code:
const int zero = 0;
int* p = zero;
options: Well-formed: `zero` is an integral constant expression equal to zero
Ill-formed: `zero` is not a null pointer constant
Well-formed, but `p` holds an unspecified pointer value
questions.explanation: Since C++11 (CWG 903), a null pointer constant is an integer literal with value zero or a prvalue of type `std::nullptr_t`. `zero` is a constant expression, but it is not a literal, and there is no other conversion from `int` to `int*`, so the initialization is ill-formed. The first option describes the C++03 rule, under which any integral constant expression evaluating to zero qualified.
